opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that in RL, inference isn't a separate serving problem anymore. It *is* the training loop. Most of the wall-clock time in a large-scale RL run goes to rollouts, generating trajectories, and the policy is changing underneath you the whole time. So the inference system isn't something you build once and hand over. It's evolving together with the algorithm.

That creates a very tight coupling. Say the researchers want longer reasoning chains, or multi-turn agentic rollouts with tool calls. That immediately changes the memory profile, the batching strategy, and how you handle long-tail requests that take ten times longer than the median. On the other side, if the inference engineers do something like asynchronous rollouts, or use a slightly stale policy to keep the GPUs busy, that's no longer just an engineering optimization. It changes the off-policy-ness of your data, and it can affect training stability. Even small numerical mismatches between the inference engine and the training framework, like different kernels or precision, can show up as a mismatch in the probabilities, and suddenly your RL curve looks strange and nobody knows why.

So if the two sides sit in separate teams with a formal interface between them, you get a lot of friction. Researchers wait weeks for a feature, or engineers optimize for throughput metrics that don't actually matter for learning. The things that really move the needle are found when the same few people can look at a reward curve and a profiler trace at the same time and say, "oh, this is the bottleneck, and here's a trick that's fine algorithmically."

Agility matters because the field moves very fast. What counts as the right rollout setup changes every few months. A small, tightly knit team that can iterate daily, where the algorithm people understand the systems constraints and the systems people understand why the algorithm needs something, will usually beat a bigger team that's organized in silos. In RL especially, I think the iteration speed of the whole system *is* the research speed.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the field moves fast and that whole-system iteration speed is the research speed, linking close engineering–research coordination to rapid research progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Because in RL, inference isn't a service sitting off to the side anymore. It's inside the training loop. Every rollout the model generates is a training sample, so the throughput, the latency, the numerical behavior of the inference engine directly shape what the researcher sees in the reward curve. If those two groups are separated by a wall, you get a very slow feedback cycle: the researcher notices something strange, files a ticket, the infra person reproduces it a week later, and by then the experiment has moved on.

What actually happens in practice is that the problems are mixed. A reward that plateaus might be an algorithm issue, or it might be that the sampling kernel and the training kernel disagree in precision, so the policy you're updating isn't quite the policy that generated the data. Nobody can diagnose that from one side only. The researcher knows what the signal should look like, the inference engineer knows what the system is actually doing, and you need both people in the same room, often the same afternoon.

The other piece is that research in RL changes shape very fast. One week it's long-horizon agent trajectories with tool calls, the next week it's multi-turn with different context lengths, the next week it's a new reward model that has to run in the loop. Each of those changes the ideal scheduling, the ideal KV cache strategy, the ideal batching. If the inference team is building a general, polished system six months ahead of what research needs, half of it will be wasted, and the half that's needed won't be there. So we'd rather have a smaller team that can rewrite a piece in a few days than a large team that delivers something perfect but late.

So agility, for me, means short loops. The researcher can read the engine code, the engineer sits in the experiment review, and when something breaks, the default is that both open the same log together. That's where most of our real gains came from, not from one brilliant optimization, but from removing the delay between noticing and fixing.

r001.rationale: The response says RL research changes shape very fast and explains that close collaboration and short feedback loops let inference engineering adapt to those changing research needs.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that an RL inference system isn’t something you build once and then leave unchanged. Research keeps evolving, and that changes what you need from inference. So the team needs to be able to learn and respond quickly.

Inference engineering and research also have to work closely because their decisions affect each other. An engineering optimization might improve throughput, but we still need to understand whether it preserves the behavior the researchers need. And a research idea might look promising, but its inference cost can determine how quickly we can test and iterate on it.

That’s why I see agility and coordination as part of the system itself. The goal isn’t just to make inference fast in isolation. It’s to shorten the whole cycle—from an idea, to an experiment, to useful feedback—so that research and engineering improve together.

r001.rationale: The response says close coordination lets research and engineering improve together and shortens the cycle from idea to experiment to useful feedback, linking coordination to faster research progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that, in reinforcement learning, inference is part of the training loop. As the research changes, the workload changes, and the inference system needs to adapt with it. If engineering and research work in isolation, you can spend a lot of time optimizing something that no longer matches what the experiment needs.

So the coordination has to be very tight. Researchers need to communicate what they’re trying to learn, and inference engineers need to explain the system constraints and tradeoffs. Sometimes a research choice creates a bottleneck; sometimes an engineering improvement makes a new experiment practical. An agile team can discover those things quickly and adjust together.

Ultimately, the goal is to shorten the cycle from an idea to a useful experimental result. Raw inference throughput matters, but it matters in the context of that whole cycle.

r001.rationale: The response says tight coordination helps the team discover issues and adjust quickly, shortening the cycle from an idea to an experimental result.
